newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam keeps pressure up in China dispute.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam keeps pressure up in China dispute.

text.p: Vietnam Foreign Minister Nguyen Manh Cam has reiterated Hanoi's claim to an offshore area at the centre of an oil dispute with China after the failure of talks in Beijing last week to resolve the issue.

Cam was quoted by Monday's Saigon Times Daily as saying the waters in question belonged to Vietnam. He also called on China to comply with an agreement signed in 1991 aimed at ensuring disputes in the area are settled peacefully.

"Vietnam has respected the agreement. However, the Chinese side at times has caused problems... We call for the full implementation of these commitments and do not expect that a similar incident will happen again," he said.
The row between the two neighbours erupted in March after China's main offshore oil firm positioned its Kan Tan 111 rig in a disputed area between Hainan Island and the coast of central Vietnam.
The talks in Beijing failed to resolve the differences. A statement issued by the foreign ministry in Hanoi on Friday said no common ground had been found after three days of negotiations.
The Saigon Times Daily article said Chinese negotiators had refused to discuss the core issue of sovereignty and produced no evidence to back their claim to the area.
It also quoted Cam as saying the issue should be raised at a forthcoming meeting between members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and China.
Hanoi, which joined the seven-nation ASEAN grouping in 1995, has sought to put the issue on to a multilateral agenda and won some support for its stand from regional envoys in Hanoi last month.
The dispute is the latest in a series between the two countries, which fought a bloody border war in 1979 followed by nearly a decade of frontier hostilities.
The potential mineral wealth of offshore areas claimed by Hanoi and Beijing has been a constant threat to recent efforts by both countries to boost ties.
Both claim parts of the Tonkin Gulf and Paracel and Spratly island chains, whose ownership is also contested by a number of other regional claimants.
